name: stone
_comment: Block IDs are positional, so this entry must stay where it is; only ever APPEND new blocks.

name: surface_water
_comment: Generated ocean water, and deliberately NOT a fluid state: the flowing simulation is the dynamic water a player pours, not the sea. Left out of the state table, the ocean never ticks — it cannot spill runoff along its shores or drain through a channel — while still acting as a wall the flow pools against (see blocks_fluid in core/block_types.hpp). Adding "fluid": {"kind": "water", "depth": 0} here is what would make oceans live.

name: water
_comment: A source: the block a poured bucket places and the block a pool settles into.

name: oak_wall
_comment: A wall is a post with an arm per side it reaches toward, resolved when the chunk is meshed (core/shape_resolver.hpp): a run closes up, a wall leaning on stone runs its arm the full height, and the post keeps its top while something stands on it. The four per-material orientations all carry this one shape now  -  which way a wall runs is a property of its neighbours, not of the id you placed  -  and `_full` stays a plain cube as the way to thicken a wall into a solid block.

name: stone_wall_full
_comment: Deliberately NOT hidden, unlike the other four materials' solid walls: it is the one wall block you can still /give yourself, and it is what a pasted build turns every foreign wall into (data/minecraft_blocks.json).

name: crucible
_comment: Model: the "crucible" entry in data/block_shapes.json — 4 corner legs at full block height (1x1px, 2px tall), a 1px floor plate across the whole footprint, and 4 1px walls open at the top. The stone texture is a placeholder until the crucible has art of its own.

name: water_runoff_1
_comment: The seven runoff states and the falling state are the flowing half of water: entry order is the save-format id, so they are appended and never moved. `depth` is how many steps this water is from the source that fed it, and `falling` marks a column pouring downward (full strength; its depth is not meaningful). They are hidden from the /give list because they are what water BECOMES, not something a player places — see src/fluids/ for the rules that pick between them. Each depth has its OWN height, which is what makes a stream slope instead of sitting flat: the surface drops by (depth+1)/9, so depth 1 is 0.78 tall and depth 7 is 0.11, against the source's 0.88. The fallen state is full height, because a column of water is only ever full strength.

name: water_fallen
_comment: A column of water pouring downward: full strength all the way down, which is why this is ONE state rather than eight. Nothing reads a falling cell's depth, so there is none to store. Full height (no shape, no offset), which is what a waterfall SHOULD look like: a column, not a stack of shallow blocks.

name: lava
_comment: A source of lava: the block a poured lava bucket places. It flows exactly like water does, with three differences that live in src/fluids/fluid_rules.cpp rather than here: it stops at three cells from its source instead of seven, it waits a second between one cell and the next instead of a quarter of one, and it does not look for drops as far away. Shared with water: two side sources over solid ground DO pool into a third, so a wide enough pool of lava stops draining. NOT emissive yet — the light array is zero, so lava lights nothing; that is a deliberate follow-up rather than an oversight, since a liquid that lights the world needs the light engine to treat liquids as sources.

name: lava_runoff_1
_comment: Lava's flowing half. Only depths 1-3 exist, because three is as far as lava's traits let it spread: a depth nothing can reach needs no block to store it. The offsets are water's ladder (the surface drops by (depth+1)/9), so a stream of lava slopes exactly the way a stream of water does.

name: acid
_comment: A source of acid: the block a poured acid bucket places. It shares water's depth and reach but moves faster (three ticks a cell), and it is the one fluid that does NOT pool from a pair of side sources: two buckets do not conjure a third source, so a splash of acid spends itself and drains instead of becoming an endless supply. Everything else — the ladder of runoff depths, the falling column, the slopes — is water's, and the differences live in src/fluids/fluid_rules.cpp.

name: acid_runoff_1
_comment: Acid's flowing half: seven depths and a falling state, exactly the shape water's has, because acid's traits use water's numbers for depth and reach.

name: surface_lava
_comment: Lava a build file brought with it, left STILL: a paste places this rather than a lava source, so a pasted lake does not immediately run downhill, and `/paste <file> fluids` is what asks for the live one. It is lava to look at and lava to flow against (mesh/mesh_fluid.hpp family_of) and it declares NO fluid state, exactly like surface_water — that absence is the whole of what makes it still.

name: surface_acid
_comment: Acid a build file brought with it, left still — see surface_lava. Same substance, same shape, no fluid state.

name: oak_fence
_comment: A fence is a post with arms, not a pole: 4/16 thick where the pole is 2/16, and its collision is the post plus a raised bar per arm (1.5 high, the pole's precedent) so a body cannot hop it and the gap between rails is not a doorway. Until the neighbour resolver lands, `fence/all` draws all four arms -- correct along a run and at corners, wrong for a lone post, which is the trade the flat shape makes.

name: glass
_comment: A transparent FULL cube, like leaves: the terrain pass draws no alpha (ALPHA is 1.0 in voxel_shader.gdshader), so this reads as pale glass rather than true transparency. Its own texture rather than ice's, which would have been a stand-in that can never be told apart from ice itself.

name: glass_pane
_comment: A sheet that reaches toward another pane or toward anything offering a whole face, resolved when the chunk is meshed (core/shape_resolver.hpp). One id, no axis and no placement rule: which way the sheet runs is a property of its neighbours, so a run, a corner and a lone post are the same block. Drops itself from either orientation.

name: glass_pane_z
_comment: Kept only because block ids are positional. It was the other axis of the flat plate, chosen at placement; now that the sheet reads its own neighbours there is nothing for a second id to say, so this one carries the same shape and behaves identically wherever an old world still holds one.

name: light_torch
_comment: No `Solid` on purpose: stops_bodies() then answers false and the collision resolver skips the cell, which is what a torch does -- you walk through it. Named apart from the `torch` ITEM (data/items.json), which is the held light; a block called `torch` would have collided with it by name. The 15 is the light level the propagator reads. `drops` names the ITEM, so breaking a placed torch hands back the thing you can place again (the drop resolves after items load, see BlockRegistry::resolve_pending_drops).

name: ladder
_comment: Decorative: there is no climbing, the same reason the block-file importer skips minecraft:ladder. The other three orientations are hidden and drop this one.

name: chain
_comment: A 2/16 column, the shape a hanging chain reads as when it is one block. Its links live in the x 7..9 band of the texture, which is the region the geometry samples (see tools/make_block_textures.py).

name: lantern
_comment: Reuses the light block's art and its emissive map rather than inventing a second lamp texture: it is the same light in a smaller box.

name: carpet
_comment: A 1/16 plate. No recipe yet: there is no cloth material to cut it from, so this is the shape and the art waiting for one.

name: oak_plate
_comment: The pressure plate, named our way (the reference calls it oak_pressure_plate). Same 1/16 plate as the carpet; it is its own shape so the two can diverge.

name: snow_layer
_comment: Layer 1 of 8. The taller layers exist as blocks 2..8 (hidden) so the shape family is complete and reachable with /give; what is missing is the placement rule that GROWS an existing layer instead of stacking a second block beside it.
